about.title: Pleasant Hill Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Slip and fall incidents in Pleasant Hill happen in ordinary places — grocery stores off Taylor Boulevard, office buildings near I-680, apartment walkways, or parking lots along Contra Costa Boulevard. What separates a minor stumble from a real claim is usually notice: did the property owner know or should they have known about the wet floor, broken step, or uneven pavement, and did they fail to fix or warn about it? Contra Costa County properties vary widely in how well they're maintained, and evidence like surveillance footage or incident reports can disappear quickly once a business realizes a claim might follow. That's why documenting the scene, getting the names of witnesses, and requesting that video be preserved matters early on. LawProactive doesn't practice law or promise any result — we simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate your fall, explain California's notice requirement, and help you understand your options before the two-year deadline closes in.

whyChoose.title: Why Pleasant Hill Fall Victims Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Notice Is Everything
items.desc: California law requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney can help gather evidence — like prior complaint records or maintenance logs — to establish that notice.

items.title: Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Pleasant Hill retailers and apartment complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request preservation letters can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Doesn't End Your Claim
items.desc: Even if you were partly distracted or not watching your step, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover a share of damages reduced by your percentage of fault.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Pleasant Hill?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a public entity, such as a city building or park, the deadline is much shorter and requires an earlier claim to be filed. An attorney can confirm which timeline applies to your situation.

items.question: What if I fell at a store on Contra Costa Boulevard and I'm not sure who owns the property?
items.answer: That's common — many properties along busy corridors like Contra Costa Boulevard are leased, franchised, or managed by third parties, making ownership unclear at first glance. An independent attorney can investigate lease agreements, business registrations, and management contracts to identify the responsible party.

items.question: Will my claim be denied if I wasn't paying attention when I fell?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California uses pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover damages even if you share some responsibility for the fall, though your compensation may be reduced accordingly. The property owner's failure to fix or warn about a known hazard remains a central part of the analysis.
